topics.title: Urinary Elimination: How It Works and What Goes Wrong
topics.summary: The kidneys clean the blood and make urine. Changes in how much urine is made, or in how the bladder empties, warn you of problems.
objectives: You can explain what urinary elimination removes and why the body needs it.
You can trace urine from the kidney to the urethra.
You can name the six groups of factors that change voiding.
You can define polyuria, oliguria, anuria, frequency, nocturia, urgency, dysuria, hesitancy, and neurogenic bladder.
You can calculate minimum expected urine output with 0.5 mL/kg/hr.
You can sort urinary risk factors into ones a client can and cannot change.
topics.bigPicture:
All day long, the kidneys clean the blood. They keep what the body needs. They remove waste, extra water, and extra electrolytes. Electrolytes are charged particles, such as sodium and potassium. What is left over becomes urine.

You rarely see the kidneys. You see the result: how much urine there is, what it looks like, how often the client voids, and whether it hurts. These clues tell you about the kidneys, the body's fluid balance, and the nerves and muscles of the bladder.
recap: Elimination means getting rid of body waste. The kidneys remove dissolved waste and extra fluid; the bowel removes leftover solids.
Healthy kidneys keep ion levels right for nerves, muscles, the heart, bones, cell repair, and blood pressure.
Urine path: kidneys (nephrons) → ureters → bladder (detrusor muscle) → urethra.
Minimum urine output is 0.5 mL/kg/hr. Many nurses use 30 mL/hr as the average adult minimum.
Oliguria is less than 400 mL/day or 30 mL/hr. Anuria is less than 100 mL/day. Report both.
Polyuria is a large total volume. Frequency is voiding often, often with a normal total.
Frequency, urgency, and dysuria point to a bladder infection. Fever with flank pain suggests the kidney is involved.
Neurogenic bladder: the client cannot feel fullness and cannot control the urinary sphincters.

keyTerms.def: The secretion and excretion of body waste by the kidneys and intestines.
To urinate; the act of emptying the bladder.
Charged particles in body fluids, such as sodium, potassium, and calcium. Nerves and muscles need the right amounts.
The body's steady, balanced state.
The tiny filtering unit of the kidney. Each kidney has about a million of them.
A tiny ball of capillaries inside each nephron that filters fluid out of the blood.
How much blood the kidneys filter per minute. The best overall measure of kidney function.
The muscle wall of the bladder. It squeezes to push urine out.
A ring of muscle around the urethra that stays closed until the person decides to void.
Making abnormally large amounts of urine.
Extreme thirst. It often goes with polyuria.
Scant urine: less than 400 mL/day or less than 30 mL/hr. May signal coming kidney failure.
Less than 100 mL of urine per day.
Voiding more often than usual without a big rise in total urine.
Waking from sleep to void.
A sudden, strong need to void.
Painful or difficult voiding, often felt as burning.
Trouble or delay starting the urine stream.
A bladder that does not work right because of a nerve problem. The person cannot sense fullness or control the urinary sphincters.
The most severe form of spina bifida. The spinal cord and nerves push out through an opening in the spine.
The side of the back, below the ribs, over the kidneys.
Urine held in the bladder because it does not empty.

sections.heading: What does urinary elimination do?
sections.keyIdea: The kidneys remove dissolved waste and extra fluid from the blood; the bowel removes leftover solids.
sections.body:
Your slides define elimination as the secretion and excretion of body waste by the kidneys and intestines. In plain words, the body makes waste, and two systems get rid of it.

Each system removes something different.
bullets: Urinary elimination removes solute waste from the blood. Solutes are dissolved wastes, such as urea and creatinine.
It also removes extra liquid that is not needed for homeostasis, the body's steady state.
Bowel elimination removes the unused parts of solid food, the parts the body did not absorb.
sections.analogy: Think of the kidneys as a water plant that runs all day. Dirty water (blood) flows in. Clean water goes back into the city pipes (the bloodstream). The sludge is piped out as urine. The intestines are the trash pickup for leftover solids.

check.q: Which system removes extra water and dissolved waste from the blood?
check.a: The urinary system. The bowel removes the unused parts of solid food.

sections.heading: Why do healthy kidneys matter?
sections.keyIdea: When the kidneys fail, the whole body feels it: nerves, muscles, the heart, bones, and blood pressure.
sections.body:
Urine is not just a waste stream. By choosing what to keep and what to let go, the kidneys control the makeup of the blood. They also get rid of extra fluid and electrolytes.

Your slides list what depends on the kidneys keeping ion levels right.
bullets: Nerve and muscle function: nerves and muscles, including the heart, need the right sodium, potassium, and calcium.
Bone strength: the kidneys help balance calcium and phosphate.
Cell repair: cells need a stable setting to repair and replace themselves.
Blood pressure: by keeping or releasing water and sodium, the kidneys keep pressure steady. Then oxygen and nutrients reach the tissues.
sections.example: At the bedside: A client with kidney failure missed two dialysis visits. Both legs are swollen, the BP is 172/98, and the potassium keeps climbing. None of these look like a bladder problem. All come from kidneys that cannot remove potassium, water, and sodium. The high potassium is the most dangerous finding, because it affects the heart muscle.

sections.heading: How is urine made and released?
sections.keyIdea: Normal voiding needs three things: kidneys that make urine, nerves that sense fullness, and muscles with good tone.
sections.body:
Urine follows one path, shown in the steps below. As the bladder fills and stretches, nerves in its wall tell the brain it is getting full. The brain decides if it is a good time to go.

When it is, the detrusor muscle squeezes and the sphincters relax. Urine flows out. Until then, the brain keeps the sphincters closed.

Normal urine is clear and pale yellow to amber. A healthy adult makes about 1,200 to 1,500 mL a day, depending on intake.
steps: Kidneys sit on each side of the spine at the back of the belly. Each one filters blood through about a million nephrons.
In each nephron, the glomerulus filters fluid out of the blood. The tubules take back what the body needs, such as water, glucose, and sodium.
Ureters, two narrow tubes, carry urine down to the bladder. Waves of muscle movement push it along.
The bladder, a stretchy muscle sac, stores urine. Its wall is the detrusor muscle. An adult usually feels the urge at about 200 to 400 mL.
The urethra carries urine out. The female urethra is short (about 4 cm), one reason women get more UTIs. The male urethra is longer and passes through the prostate.
sections.analogy: Picture a water tank. The kidneys are the pipe that fills it. The detrusor is the tank squeezing, and the sphincter is the valve. The nerves are a float sensor wired to the control room, the brain. Cut the wire, and the brain never learns the tank is full. That is a neurogenic bladder.

check.q: Which structure stores urine, and what is its muscle called?
check.a: The bladder stores urine. Its muscle wall is the detrusor, which squeezes to empty it.

sections.heading: What changes how a client voids?
sections.keyIdea: Six groups of factors change voiding: intake, muscle tone, feelings, disease, procedures, and medications.
sections.body:
Your slides list six groups of factors. Knowing them helps you ask the right questions and predict problems.

Simple fixes come first. A client who cannot start the stream on a bedpan may just need privacy and a normal position. If allowed, help the client sit on a commode or stand.

rows: Fluid and food intake
More fluid means more urine. Caffeine and alcohol raise output. Salty foods make the body hold water.
Muscle tone
Weak pelvic floor or bladder muscles make it hard to hold urine or empty fully. Causes include childbirth, aging, and long-term catheters.
Psychosocial factors
Anxiety, no privacy, or having to use a bedpan can make it hard to start voiding.
Disease (pathologic conditions)
Diabetes, kidney disease, an enlarged prostate, stroke, or spinal cord injury can change how much urine is made or how the bladder empties.
Surgery and tests
Anesthesia and pain drugs dull bladder signals, so retention is common after surgery. Some tests limit fluids or use contrast dye.
Medications
Diuretics raise output. Anticholinergics and opioids can cause retention. Some drugs change urine color.

sections.example: At the bedside: Six hours after hip surgery under spinal anesthesia, a client has not voided. She has had IV fluids and morphine. You feel a firm, rounded swelling above the pubic bone. Anesthesia, opioids, and lying flat all dull the urge. You suspect urinary retention and check her bladder with a bladder scan per protocol.

sections.heading: Too much urine or too little?
sections.keyIdea: Oliguria and anuria can mean the kidneys are failing; polyuria can drain the body of fluid.
sections.body:
Some problems change how much urine the kidneys make. The word parts help. Poly means much, oligo means little, and an means none.

When the kidneys make almost nothing, fluid and electrolytes build up. Expect weight gain, edema, high blood pressure, and a high potassium level.

rows: Polyuria (diuresis)
Abnormally large amounts of urine
Fluid loss leads to intense thirst, dehydration, and weight loss. Causes include uncontrolled diabetes, diuretics, and large intake.
Polydipsia
Extreme thirst
Goes with polyuria; the body is replacing lost water. Do not limit fluids on your own. Find the cause.
Oliguria
Less than 400 mL/day or less than 30 mL/hr
May signal coming kidney failure or dehydration. Report it.
Anuria
Less than 100 mL/day
The kidneys are making almost nothing. Report it promptly.

check.q: A client made 340 mL of urine in 24 hours. Is this oliguria or anuria?
check.a: Oliguria. It is less than 400 mL/day but more than 100 mL/day.

sections.heading: How much urine is enough?
sections.keyIdea: Expect at least 0.5 mL of urine per kilogram per hour, and always do the math with the client's real weight.
sections.body:
Your slides give a formula for the minimum expected output: 0.5 mL/kg/hr. Many nurses use 30 mL/hr as the average adult minimum. But a large client needs more than 30 mL/hr.

Output below the expected amount for 2 hours or more needs follow-up. With a catheter, check the tubing for kinks first. Then assess fluid status and notify the provider.
steps: Find the weight in kilograms (pounds ÷ 2.2).
Multiply by 0.5 to get the minimum mL per hour.
Multiply by the hours you are reviewing, such as 8 for a shift.
Compare the real output with that minimum.
sections.example: At the bedside: A client weighs 80 kg. The minimum is 80 × 0.5 = 40 mL/hr, or 320 mL in 8 hours. The bag holds 150 mL after 8 hours. That is about 19 mL/hr. You make sure the tubing is not kinked. Then you look for signs of dehydration and notify the provider.

check.q: What is the minimum hourly urine output for a 60-kg client?

sections.heading: Is the bladder emptying normally?
sections.keyIdea: Some problems leave the amount of urine normal but change how, when, or how comfortably the bladder empties.
sections.body: These problems are about emptying, not making urine. Your slides list the terms below. Learn what each one sounds like when a client describes it.
bullets: Frequency: voiding more often than usual, such as every hour, without a big rise in total output.
Nocturia: waking from sleep to void.
Urgency: a sudden, strong need to void.
Dysuria: painful or hard voiding, often burning. A common sign of a urinary tract infection (UTI).
Hesitancy: trouble or delay starting the stream. Common with an enlarged prostate, which squeezes the urethra.
Neurogenic bladder: a nerve problem. The client cannot sense fullness or control the sphincters, so the bladder may leak or over-fill.
sections.example: At the bedside: A 24-year-old woman says she voids every 30 minutes. She passes small amounts, it burns, and she cannot wait once the urge hits. Frequency, urgency, and dysuria suggest a bladder infection. You ask about fever and flank pain, which would suggest the kidney is involved. You expect a urinalysis and a urine culture.

sections.heading: Which risk factors can be changed?
sections.keyIdea: Nonmodifiable risks cannot be changed; modifiable risks can, so aim your teaching at them.
sections.body:
Nonmodifiable risk factors are ones the client cannot change. Modifiable risk factors can be changed or managed. The table sorts the ones from your slides.

Elimination also links to other concepts. These include cognition, fluids and electrolytes, infection, inflammation, mobility, and teaching and learning. A problem in any of them can show up as an elimination problem.

rows: Physical, cognitive, or developmental disability
Obesity, which puts extra pressure on the bladder
Family history of incontinence
Pregnancy
Spina bifida, including myelomeningocele; nerve damage often causes a neurogenic bladder
Medical procedures that need anesthesia
Aging, and diseases such as Parkinson and Alzheimer disease
Medications taken for other conditions, such as diuretics or sedatives
Men: an enlarged prostate that squeezes the urethra
Poor hygiene, which raises infection risk
Women: weak muscles that support the bladder or sphincter. Both: smaller bladder capacity
Lower income and education, which can limit access to care and health information

sections.example: At the bedside: An 84-year-old with dementia had a hip fracture repaired. She is wet at almost every check, and her urinalysis is normal. Her bladder may be fine. The real problems are cognition (she does not notice the urge) and mobility (she cannot get up alone). The plan is scheduled, assisted toileting, not a device.

sections.heading: Common traps: look-alikes to tell apart
sections.keyIdea: Many wrong answers swap one close term for another, so check the amount, the timing, and the cause.

rows: Polyuria vs frequency
Polyuria is a large total volume. Frequency is voiding often; the total may be normal.
Oliguria vs anuria
Oliguria is under 400 mL/day or 30 mL/hr. Anuria is under 100 mL/day.
Polyuria vs polydipsia
Polyuria is too much urine. Polydipsia is too much thirst.
30 mL/hr vs 0.5 mL/kg/hr
30 mL/hr is only an average. A 100-kg client needs at least 50 mL/hr.
Kidney failure vs a blocked catheter
Low output in a bag? Check for kinks and loops first. Then report a possible kidney problem.
Bladder vs kidney infection
Burning, frequency, and urgency suggest the bladder. Fever with flank pain suggests the kidney.
Bladder problem vs toileting problem
A normal urinalysis with dementia or poor mobility calls for toileting help, not a catheter.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Expect output math, term matching, and "which client first" items built on low urine output.
sections.body:
Sample: The nurse reviews 4-hour urine totals for four adults after surgery. Which client needs follow-up first?

A. 50 kg, 120 mL
B. 100 kg, 140 mL
C. 60 kg, 130 mL
D. 70 kg, 160 mL
bullets: Output math: weight × 0.5 × hours, then compare with the real total.
Term matching: oliguria, anuria, polyuria, frequency, dysuria.
Priority: low output, anuria, or high potassium in kidney failure.
Select all: what raises urine output, or what causes retention after surgery.
steps: Read the stem: four clients, four weights, four totals over 4 hours.
What is it really asking? Which client is below 0.5 mL/kg/hr.
Key cues: the weights differ, so 30 mL/hr is not the right yardstick for everyone.
Why the others are wrong: A needs 25 mL/hr and makes 30. C needs 30 and makes about 32. D needs 35 and makes 40.
The answer is B. This client needs 50 mL/hr but makes only 35. It looks fine by the 30 mL/hr rule, which is the trap.
Strategy: when weights are given, always do the weight-based math. Never stop at 30 mL/hr.

sections.heading: Worked case: low output the day after surgery
sections.keyIdea: Rule out a blocked catheter first, then report low output with rising kidney labs to the provider.
sections.body: A 70-kg client had surgery yesterday and has an indwelling catheter. Output has been 25 mL/hr for 3 hours. The tubing is straight and draining freely. Today's BUN is 32 mg/dL, up from 18. The creatinine has also gone up.
steps: Recognize cues: 25 mL/hr for 3 hours, plus a rising BUN and creatinine.
Do the math: 70 × 0.5 = 35 mL/hr. The client is below it.
Rule out the simple cause: the catheter is not kinked or blocked.
Assess fluid status: intake, weight, BP, pulse, skin, mouth, and edema.
Act: notify the provider. Low output with rising kidney labs may signal kidney injury.
Evaluate: keep tracking hourly output and the labs.

check.q: Why is "recheck in 4 hours" the wrong choice?
check.a: Output has been low for more than 2 hours, and kidney labs are rising. Waiting delays care for possible kidney failure.

mnemonics.name: Word parts for urine terms
mnemonics.text: Poly = much (polyuria, polydipsia). Oligo = little (oliguria). An = none (anuria). Dys = painful (dysuria). Noct = night (nocturia).

pearls: Do the 0.5 mL/kg/hr math whenever a weight is given. Large clients need more than 30 mL/hr.
For low output with a catheter, check the tubing and bag before you think kidney failure.
Polyuria and polydipsia travel together: the client drinks because they are losing water. Do not limit fluids on your own; look for a cause, such as high blood glucose.
Privacy and a normal voiding position come before any catheter.
In kidney failure, a high potassium is the finding most likely to kill quickly.
Anesthesia, opioids, anticholinergics, and bedpan use all promote retention after surgery.
redFlags: Output below 0.5 mL/kg/hr (or 30 mL/hr) for 2 hours or more → check the catheter, assess fluid status, and notify the provider.
Less than 100 mL of urine in 24 hours (anuria) → notify the provider promptly; the kidneys may be failing.
Intense thirst, large urine volumes, and weight loss → assess for dehydration and report. Check blood glucose if ordered.
Burning with fever and flank pain → the kidney may be involved; report promptly.

checks.q: A 92-kg client has made 110 mL of urine in 4 hours. Is this enough?
checks.a: No. The minimum is 92 × 0.5 = 46 mL/hr, or 184 mL in 4 hours. 110 mL is about 27 mL/hr. Check the catheter, assess the client, and notify the provider.

checks.q: A client voids every hour, but the 24-hour total is 1,350 mL. Is this polyuria?
checks.a: No. The total is normal, so this is frequency. Polyuria means a large total volume.

checks.q: A client with a spinal cord injury does not feel the need to void and leaks without warning. What is this called?
checks.a: Neurogenic bladder. The client cannot sense fullness or control the urinary sphincters.

checks.q: Name three things that must work together for normal voiding.
checks.a: Kidneys that make urine, nerves that sense fullness and signal the muscles, and bladder and pelvic floor muscles with good tone.

checks.q: A woman asks why she gets UTIs and her husband does not. What is a key reason?
checks.a: The female urethra is short, about 4 cm. Bacteria have a shorter trip to the bladder.

topics.title: Urinary Assessment, Tests, and Kidney Labs
topics.summary: Assessment starts with direct questions and a focused exam. Urine tests, imaging, scopes, and blood work then show how well the kidneys and bladder work.
objectives: You can list what to ask and what to examine in a urinary assessment.
You can explain why incontinence and retention are never normal at any age.
You can describe the purpose of a urinalysis, urine culture, post-void residual, bladder scan, PSA, and stress test.
You can give safe care before and after an IVP, cystoscopy, and kidney biopsy.
You can state normal BUN, creatinine, GFR, creatinine clearance, and specific gravity, and read changes.
topics.bigPicture:
Urinary problems are often hidden. Many clients feel embarrassed to talk about leaking or trouble voiding. Many think it is just part of getting older. If you do not ask, you may never find out.

Once a problem is suspected, tests show where it is. It may be in the kidneys, which make urine. It may be in the bladder and urethra, which store and release it. Or it may be the prostate, which can block it. Some tests carry real risks, such as dye reactions or bleeding. The nurse prepares the client and catches problems early.
recap: There is no standard screening test. Ask direct, specific questions, especially with older adults.
Urinary incontinence and retention are never normal at any age. They often point to another problem.
Collect a urine culture before the first antibiotic dose.
Measure a post-void residual right after voiding, best with a bladder scan.
Before contrast (IVP): ask about metformin, past dye reactions, iodine or shellfish allergy, and asthma. Report all of them.
After cystoscopy, pink urine and mild burning are expected. Bright red urine, clots, fever, or no voiding are not.
Kidney biopsy means bleeding risk. A rising pulse and falling BP mean bleeding until proven otherwise.
BUN 8–20 and creatinine 0.5–1.2 go up in kidney disease. GFR (90–110) and creatinine clearance (80–140) go down.

keyTerms.def: A lab exam of urine for color, clarity, specific gravity, pH, and abnormal contents such as protein, glucose, blood, white blood cells, or bacteria.
A test that grows bacteria from urine. It names the germ causing an infection and which antibiotics will work.
A urine sample taken from the middle of the stream after cleansing, to cut down on skin germs.
The amount of urine left in the bladder right after the person voids.
A painless, portable ultrasound that estimates how much urine is in the bladder.
A blood test for a protein made by the prostate. It rises with an enlarged prostate, inflammation, or prostate cancer.
A test for leaking. The client coughs or bears down with a full bladder while the examiner watches.
An x-ray study of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder using IV contrast dye.
A liquid given by IV that shows up on x-ray or CT. The kidneys must filter it out.
A dangerous buildup of acid in the blood. Metformin can cause it if the kidneys cannot clear the drug.
A plain x-ray of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder. No dye and no special preparation.
A lighted scope passed through the urethra to look inside the bladder.
A needle removes a small piece of kidney tissue to study. The main risk is bleeding.
Blood in the urine.
The opening of the urethra on the outside of the body.
A waste product of protein breakdown that the kidneys clear. Normal 8–20 mg/dL.
A waste product of muscle activity that the kidneys must remove. Normal serum level 0.5–1.2 mg/dL.
A test comparing creatinine in the blood with creatinine in a 24-hour urine. Normal 80–140 mL/min.
How concentrated urine is compared with water. Normal 1.005–1.030.

sections.heading: How do you start a urinary assessment?
sections.keyIdea: There is no standard screening test, so the nurse screens by asking direct, specific questions.
sections.body:
Your slides split the assessment into two parts: observation and interview, then the physical exam. Give privacy and use a calm, matter-of-fact tone.

There are no standard screening tests for urinary problems. Screening is verbal, during regular checkups, especially for older adults. Urinary problems need more direct questions than other problems, because clients are embarrassed.

Remember: incontinence and retention are never normal, at any age. They often point to another problem, such as an infection, a drug effect, an enlarged prostate, nerve disease, or constipation.
bullets: Voiding pattern: How often do you void by day? At night? Has that changed?
Urine and any changes: color, clarity, odor, amount, blood.
Problems: burning, urgency, leaking, trouble starting, a weak stream, not emptying fully.
Influencing factors: fluids (including caffeine and alcohol), medicines, recent procedures, mobility, and illnesses such as diabetes.
sections.example: At the bedside: A 70-year-old woman says no when asked, "Any bladder problems?" The nurse then asks, "Do you ever leak when you cough or laugh? Do you wear a pad?" She says yes to both. Specific questions make it easier to admit a problem.

check.q: An 80-year-old says, "Leaking is just part of getting old." How do you respond?
check.a: Explain that incontinence is never a normal part of aging. It often has a cause that can be treated, so it is worth checking.

sections.heading: What do you check in the exam?
sections.keyIdea: Look at the abdomen, the skin and genitals, the urethral opening, stool and urine, and fluid status.
sections.body:
Your slides list five areas to examine.

Fever with flank tenderness is important. It suggests the infection has reached the kidney. Report it promptly.
bullets: Abdomen: a rounded swelling above the pubic bone suggests a full bladder. It may feel firm, and pressing may cause discomfort or an urge.
Genitals and perianal skin: redness, rash, skin breakdown from urine, discharge, or swelling.
Urethral meatus: redness, discharge, or swelling.
Feces and urine: constipation can press on the bladder. Urine should be clear and pale yellow.
Fluid volume status: daily weight, intake and output, skin turgor, mucous membranes, edema, BP, and pulse.
sections.example: At the bedside: An older man in long-term care is wet all day and restless. The nurse feels a firm mass above his pubic bone. Leaking plus a full bladder suggests the bladder is over-filling and spilling over. The nurse does a bladder scan and reports the result.

sections.heading: Which urine and bladder tests will you see?
sections.keyIdea: Collect a culture before antibiotics, and measure a post-void residual right after the client voids.
sections.body:
Your slides list several tests that look at urine and the bladder. The table shows what each one tells you and what the nurse does.

A large post-void residual means the bladder is not emptying. Report it, especially in a man with an enlarged prostate.

rows: Urinalysis
Color, clarity, specific gravity, pH, protein, glucose, blood, WBCs, bacteria
Use a fresh clean-catch specimen. Send it promptly.
Urine culture
Which bacteria are present and which antibiotics will work
Use sterile technique. Collect it before the first antibiotic dose.
Post-void residual (PVR)
Urine left in the bladder after voiding
Measure right after voiding, by bladder scan or straight catheter.
Bladder scan
How much urine is in the bladder
Painless and noninvasive. No catheter infection risk.
PSA
A prostate protein in the blood
High with an enlarged prostate, inflammation, or prostate cancer.
Urinary stress test
Whether urine leaks when belly pressure rises
The client coughs or bears down with a full bladder while the examiner watches.

steps: Clean catch: clean the area around the urethral opening.
Start the stream into the toilet.
Catch the middle part of the stream in the sterile cup.
Finish voiding in the toilet, and send the cup promptly.

check.q: Why collect a urine culture before the first antibiotic dose?
check.a: The antibiotic starts killing the bacteria. A culture taken after it may not grow the germ, giving a false or misleading result.

sections.heading: How do you read a urinalysis?
sections.keyIdea: Normal urine has no glucose, no blood, no bacteria, few or no WBCs, and no protein or only a trace.
sections.body:
Healthy urine is clear and pale yellow to amber, with a faint smell. Dark amber urine is usually concentrated, as in dehydration. Cloudy, foul-smelling urine suggests infection.

The table shows normal results and what to think about when they are off.

rows: Specific gravity
High: dehydration. Low: dilute urine from large intake or kidneys that cannot concentrate.
Glucose
None
High blood glucose spilling into urine, as in uncontrolled diabetes
Protein
None or trace
Damage to the kidney filters
Blood (hematuria)
None
Infection, kidney stones, injury, or a recent procedure such as cystoscopy
WBCs and bacteria
None or few
Urinary tract infection; a culture names the germ

sections.example: At the bedside: An older client has cloudy urine with many WBCs and bacteria, plus new confusion. In older adults, confusion may be the first sign of a UTI, not burning or fever. The nurse makes sure a culture was sent before antibiotics and reports the results.

sections.heading: Why is contrast dye a safety risk?
sections.keyIdea: Contrast dye stresses the kidneys, so check metformin, allergies, and kidney labs before it is given.
sections.body:
An IVP uses IV contrast dye to outline the kidneys, ureters, and bladder on x-ray. The kidneys must filter the dye out. That creates two safety issues on your slides.

Metformin: your slides say to stop it 48 hours before the test. If dye stresses the kidneys, metformin can build up and cause lactic acidosis. Newer guidelines focus more on the time after the test. Metformin is held at the time of the test and for 48 hours after. It restarts only once kidney function is rechecked and stable. Follow facility protocol.

Allergies: ask about iodine or shellfish allergy, past dye reactions, and asthma. A past dye reaction is the strongest predictor of another one. A shellfish allergy alone does not mean the client will react, but still ask and report it.
bullets: Report worsening kidney labs before any study with IV contrast.
During injection, itching, hives, wheezing, or a tight throat means a reaction. Stop the infusion if able, stay with the client, and call for help.
After the test, encourage fluids (if allowed) to help flush the dye.
sections.example: At the bedside: A client scheduled for an IVP tomorrow took his metformin with breakfast. He says he broke out in hives after eating shrimp. The nurse holds further doses and confirms his allergy history. The nurse notifies the provider and radiology so they can decide whether to proceed.

sections.heading: What about KUB, cystoscopy, and kidney biopsy?
sections.keyIdea: A KUB needs no prep, cystoscopy can cause bleeding and burning, and kidney biopsy carries a real risk of bleeding.
sections.body:
Your slides list more tests, from simple x-rays to invasive procedures. Noninvasive tests include ultrasound, CT, MRI, and renal scan. They show structure and blood flow without entering the body. Some CT scans use contrast, so the same dye safety checks apply.

The kidney is full of blood vessels. That is why bleeding is the big worry after a biopsy.
bullets: KUB: a plain belly x-ray with no dye. It shows organ size, position, and some kidney stones. No special prep.
Cystoscopy, after: watch for swelling, dysuria, and hematuria. Pink urine and mild burning are common for a short time. Encourage fluids unless restricted.
Cystoscopy, report: bright red urine, clots, fever, or not being able to void.
Kidney biopsy, before: check clotting labs as ordered. Report anything that impairs clotting, such as anticoagulants or a high INR.
Kidney biopsy, after: watch vital signs, the site, and the urine for blood. Keep the client on bed rest as ordered.

check.q: After a kidney biopsy, the pulse rises from 78 to 112 and the BP drops from 128/76 to 98/60. What do you suspect?
check.a: Bleeding. Keep the client flat, check the site and urine, and notify the provider immediately.

sections.heading: What do the kidney labs tell you?
sections.keyIdea: BUN and creatinine go up when the kidneys fail; GFR and creatinine clearance go down.
sections.body:
Blood tests show how well the kidneys filter. Your slides give the normal values in the table. Creatinine is the more specific marker of kidney function. BUN also rises with dehydration.

So compare them. A high BUN and specific gravity with a normal creatinine points to dehydration, not kidney damage.

rows: BUN
8–20 mg/dL
Up in kidney disease. Also up with dehydration.
Serum creatinine
Up in kidney disease. The more specific kidney marker.
GFR
90–110 mL/min
Falls when kidneys fail. Also diminishes with age.
Creatinine clearance
80–140 mL/min
Falls when kidneys cannot clear creatinine. Needs a 24-hour urine.
Specific gravity
Up with dehydration (concentrated urine). Low means dilute urine.

sections.analogy: Creatinine is like trash a house makes at a steady rate. If the garbage truck (the kidneys) stops coming, trash piles up in the house. Blood creatinine rises. Less trash reaches the dump, so urine creatinine falls.
sections.example: At the bedside: A client has vomited for 2 days and has a dry mouth. Her specific gravity is 1.035, BUN is 28 mg/dL, and creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. The high specific gravity and BUN with a normal creatinine suggest dehydration. The nurse reports the findings and expects fluid replacement.

sections.heading: How does a creatinine clearance test work?
sections.keyIdea: Working kidneys move creatinine into the urine, so clearance falls when the kidneys fail.
sections.body:
The kidneys must remove creatinine from the body. This test compares creatinine in the blood with creatinine in the urine over 24 hours. If the kidneys work, the level is higher in the urine. The test shows how much kidney function is lost.

One caution: your slide lists "increased in renal disease" beside creatinine clearance. That label fits BUN and serum creatinine. Clearance itself goes down in kidney disease.
steps: Have the client void and discard that first urine. Note the time. The test starts now.
Save all urine for the next 24 hours. Keep it on ice or refrigerated.
At the end time, have the client void one last time and add that urine.
A blood creatinine is drawn during the test.
If any void is thrown away, restart the collection and tell the lab.

check.q: At 1400, an aide flushed a void during a 24-hour collection that began at 0700. What now?
check.a: The collection is incomplete. Restart it with a new start time, and tell the lab.

sections.heading: Common traps: look-alikes to tell apart
sections.keyIdea: Most wrong answers mix up which labs rise and which fall, or what is expected versus reportable.

rows: Serum creatinine vs creatinine clearance
Serum creatinine goes up in kidney disease. Clearance goes down.
Dehydration vs kidney damage
Dehydration: high BUN and specific gravity, normal creatinine. Kidney damage: BUN and creatinine both high.
Expected vs reportable after cystoscopy
Pink urine and mild burning are expected. Bright red urine, clots, fever, or no voiding are not.
Shellfish allergy vs past dye reaction
Both are reported. A past dye reaction is the strongest predictor of another reaction.
Retention vs low output
Retention: a full bladder on scan. Low output with high specific gravity and an empty bladder: fluid deficit.
First void vs last void in a 24-hour urine
Discard the first void. Add the last one.
Normal aging vs incontinence
Lower GFR with age is normal. Incontinence and retention never are.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Expect pre-test safety checks, post-procedure priorities, lab reading, and teaching for specimen collection.
sections.body:
Sample: Two hours after a kidney biopsy, the client says, "I feel lightheaded." Pulse was 80 and is now 116. BP was 130/78 and is now 96/58. What should the nurse do first?

A. Give the prescribed oral pain medicine
B. Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees
C. Keep the client flat and notify the provider
D. Encourage oral fluids and recheck in an hour
bullets: Before contrast: which findings to report (metformin, allergies, asthma, kidney labs).
After a procedure: which finding needs follow-up first.
Labs: select all that are abnormal; dehydration vs kidney disease.
Teaching: "needs more teaching" about clean catch or a 24-hour urine.
steps: Read the stem: a fresh kidney biopsy, a faster pulse, a lower BP, and lightheadedness.
What is it really asking? What is happening, and what is the first safe action.
Key cues: biopsy means bleeding risk. Pulse up and BP down is the body losing blood.
Why the others are wrong: A treats pain, not bleeding. B lowers blood flow to the brain and can make dizziness worse. D delays care.
The answer is C. Keep the client flat and get the provider now.
Strategy: after any invasive test, link the test to its main risk. Then pick the action that treats that risk now.

sections.heading: Worked case: IVP prep with diabetes
sections.keyIdea: Before contrast, find and report every risk: metformin, allergies, asthma, and kidney function.
sections.body: A 67-year-old client with type 2 diabetes is scheduled for an IVP tomorrow. She takes metformin twice a day. She has asthma and once had hives after eating shrimp. Today's creatinine is 1.4 mg/dL, up from 1.0 last month.
steps: Recognize cues: metformin, asthma, a shellfish reaction, and a rising creatinine.
Analyze: dye stresses the kidneys. With weaker kidneys, metformin can build up and cause lactic acidosis.
Act: hold metformin per protocol.
Report all four findings to the provider and radiology before the test.
After the test: encourage fluids if allowed. Do not restart metformin until kidney function is rechecked and stable.

check.q: That night after the IVP, the client says, "I feel fine. Can I take my metformin?" The repeat creatinine is not back yet. What do you say?
check.a: Not yet. Metformin restarts only after kidney function is rechecked and stable.

pearls: Ask specific, direct questions about leaking and voiding; clients rarely volunteer urinary symptoms.
Incontinence and retention are never normal at any age. Look for the cause.
Kidney biopsy equals bleeding risk. Watch vital signs, the site, and the urine.
High specific gravity means concentrated urine. Think dehydration.
Fever with flank tenderness suggests the kidney is involved. Report it promptly.
redFlags: Rising pulse, falling BP, or blood in the urine after kidney biopsy → suspect bleeding; keep flat and notify the provider immediately.
Bright red urine, clots, fever, or not able to void after cystoscopy → report promptly.
Itching, hives, wheezing, or a tight throat during dye injection → stop the infusion if able, stay with the client, and call for help.
Anticoagulant use or a high INR before a kidney biopsy → report before the procedure.

checks.q: A client's BUN is 42 mg/dL and creatinine is 3.1 mg/dL. What do these suggest?
checks.a: Both are high, which suggests kidney disease (impaired kidney function).

checks.q: A man voids 150 mL and still feels full. A bladder scan right after shows 420 mL. What does this mean?
checks.a: A large post-void residual. His bladder is not emptying. Report it, especially with an enlarged prostate.

checks.q: Why does an 85-year-old have a lower GFR than a 25-year-old with no kidney disease?
checks.a: GFR normally diminishes with age as blood flow to the kidneys decreases.

checks.q: A client has low output, specific gravity 1.034, a fast pulse, and an empty bladder on scan. Retention or fluid deficit?
checks.a: Fluid deficit. Retention would show a full bladder. Concentrated urine and a fast pulse point to low fluid volume.

topics.title: Urinary Care, Medications, and Dialysis
topics.summary: Nurses support urinary health with fluids, accurate intake and output, clean catheter care, and teaching. The team adds bladder drugs, diuretics, and dialysis when needed.
objectives: You can list independent nursing actions for clients with urinary problems.
You can explain why catheter care needs aseptic technique and daily review.
You can match each urinary drug class with its purpose, example, and key caution.
You can give loop, thiazide, and potassium-sparing diuretics safely.
You can compare hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis.
You can teach habits that prevent urinary problems.
topics.bigPicture:
Your slides say care depends on the cause and severity of the problem. A mild bladder infection needs fluids, antibiotics, and teaching. Kidneys that have failed need dialysis to keep the client alive. Most clients are somewhere in between.

Care comes in two groups. Independent actions are ones the nurse starts without an order, like encouraging fluids. Collaborative care involves the team: drugs, referrals, and dialysis. The nurse plays a part in both, especially in giving drugs safely and spotting side effects.
recap: Independent care: fluids, intake and output, catheter care, teaching, and incontinence care. Aseptic technique is essential.
Keep the drainage bag below the bladder. Ask every day if the catheter is still needed.
Ditropan (anticholinergic) calms the bladder. Avoid in glaucoma. Watch for retention, constipation, and confusion.
Urecholine (cholinergic) helps the bladder empty. It can raise liver and pancreatic enzymes.
Pyridium treats pain only and turns urine orange-red. The antibiotic must be finished.
Lasix, HCTZ, Aldactone: check BUN, creatinine, K⁺, and Na⁺. Aldactone keeps potassium, so no salt substitutes.
Hemodialysis filters blood in a machine. Peritoneal dialysis uses solution placed in the abdomen.
Protect a fistula arm: no BP, blood draws, or IVs. Feel the thrill and hear the bruit.

keyTerms.def: An action the nurse can start on their own, based on nursing judgment.
Care planned with other team members, such as medications, referrals, or dialysis.
Measuring all fluid taken in and all fluid lost, such as urine, vomit, and drainage.
Practices that keep germs out of the body, such as hand hygiene and keeping catheter equipment clean or sterile.
A tube left in the bladder to drain urine into a bag.
A drug that blocks the nerve signal that makes the bladder squeeze. Used to reduce frequency and treat incontinence.
A drug that mimics the nerve signal that makes the bladder squeeze. Used to promote urination.
The chemical messenger nerves use to tell the bladder muscle to squeeze.
An eye disease with high pressure inside the eye. Anticholinergics can raise that pressure.
A drug that makes the kidneys remove more water and sodium, so urine output rises.
A diuretic that keeps potassium in the body instead of losing it in urine.
A seasoning made of potassium chloride instead of sodium. Risky with potassium-sparing diuretics.
Blood flows through an outside machine that filters it, then returns to the body.
Solution is placed in the abdomen. It pulls wastes and fluid from the blood and is then drained.
A surgical joining of an artery and vein, usually in the arm, used for hemodialysis access.
A thrill is the buzz you feel over a working fistula. A bruit is the whoosh you hear with a stethoscope.

sections.heading: What can the nurse do without an order?
sections.keyIdea: Fluids, accurate I&O, clean catheter care, teaching, and skin care are the core independent actions.
sections.body:
Your slides list the core independent actions below. They prevent many problems before drugs are ever needed.

Fluids come first for most clients. Unless fluids are restricted, as in heart or kidney failure, encourage about 2 L or more a day, spread out. Good intake dilutes urine and flushes bacteria out of the bladder.
bullets: Increase fluid intake unless restricted.
Monitor I&O. Output well below intake, or below 0.5 mL/kg/hr, needs follow-up.
Catheter care: bag below the bladder and off the floor, tubing free of kinks, clean the area, empty the bag regularly.
Teaching: fluids, hygiene, medicines, signs of infection, and devices at home.
Incontinence care: keep skin clean and dry, use barrier products, change briefs promptly, offer the toilet on a schedule.
Aseptic technique in all catheter care. Urinary catheters are a leading source of health care–associated infections.
sections.example: At the bedside: An aide has hooked a client's drainage bag to the bed rail at hip level. Urine sits in a loop of tubing. You step in right away. You lower the bag below the bladder and straighten the tubing. Now urine drains by gravity and cannot flow back into the bladder.

sections.heading: How do you keep a catheter infection-free?
sections.keyIdea: Insert with sterile technique, keep the system closed, and remove the catheter as soon as it is not needed.
sections.body:
The bladder is normally sterile. A catheter is a highway from the outside world into it. Germs can travel up the outside of the tube. They can also travel up the inside if the system is opened or urine flows back.

That is why you insert catheters with sterile technique and keep the system closed. The best prevention is a short catheter time. Ask every day whether it is still needed. Remind the provider when it may not be.

Fever and flank pain in a client with a catheter suggest infection. See that client before routine catheter fixes.
sections.analogy: A catheter is like propping open the front door of a clean house. The longer it stays open, the more likely something unwanted wanders in.

check.q: On day 3 after surgery, a client walks the hall alone and still has the catheter placed for surgery. There is no order about it. What do you do?
check.a: Ask the provider whether the catheter is still needed. Prompt removal lowers infection risk.

sections.heading: Who else helps the client?
sections.keyIdea: Plan referrals before discharge so supplies, skills, and support are in place when the client gets home.
sections.body:
Many clients go home or to a facility still managing a urinary problem. Your slides list referrals before or after discharge. They say teamwork is especially important in long-term care or assisted living.

Include family members and caregivers in teaching early. They help with toileting, skin care, and devices.

rows: Wound and ostomy nurse
Skin care for incontinence, urinary diversions, and complex catheter or skin problems
Occupational therapist (OT)
Safe toileting: transfers, adaptive clothing, raised toilet seats, grab bars
Home health nurse
Catheter care, teaching, and assessment at home
Medical supply company
Catheters, drainage bags, absorbent products, commodes
Family and caregivers
Learn to help with toileting, skin care, and devices

sections.example: At the bedside: A client recovering from a stroke is going home. He has trouble getting on and off the toilet. He needs grab bars, a raised seat, and help with transfers. You refer him to occupational therapy.

sections.heading: How do you measure I&O accurately?
sections.keyIdea: I&O only helps if it is complete: count every fluid in and out, and measure instead of guessing.
sections.body: I&O shows whether fluid going in matches fluid coming out. It is often where kidney problems, dehydration, or fluid overload first show up. It must be complete and accurate.
steps: Count all intake: oral fluids, foods liquid at room temperature (ice chips, gelatin, ice cream, soup), IV fluids, and tube feedings.
Count all output: urine, vomit, liquid stool, and drainage from tubes or wounds.
Measure, do not guess. Use a graduated container, not bag or urinal markings. Read it at eye level.
Teach the client and family to save urine in the hat, urinal, or bedpan and to report what they drink.
Total and compare each shift and every 24 hours. Compare output with 0.5 mL/kg/hr and with daily weight.
sections.example: At the bedside: After 12 hours, a 70-kg client took in 2,100 mL (1,200 oral and 900 IV). Urine output is only 360 mL. The minimum is 35 mL/hr, or 420 mL in 12 hours. You check for swelling and lung crackles. Then you report the low output and the gap to the provider.

sections.heading: Which drugs calm or empty the bladder?
sections.keyIdea: Anticholinergics block the "squeeze" signal and calm the bladder; cholinergics boost it and help the bladder empty.
sections.body:
The bladder's "empty now" signal travels on nerves that use acetylcholine. That makes two opposite drug groups easy to sort.

Anticholinergics block the signal, so the bladder relaxes. Too much causes the opposite problem: retention. The same blocking dries the mouth, slows the gut, blurs vision, and can raise eye pressure. That is why they are avoided in glaucoma.

Cholinergics boost the signal, so the bladder squeezes. They help when the bladder will not empty. Success is good voiding with a low residual. Before the first dose, report asthma, a blockage of urine flow, high liver enzymes, or a slow heart rate.

rows: Anticholinergic
Reduce frequency; treat incontinence
Ditropan (oxybutynin): significant side effects, such as dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, retention, and confusion in older adults. Avoid in glaucoma.
Cholinergic
Promote urination in retention
Urecholine (bethanechol): can raise liver and pancreatic enzymes. Not for a blocked outflow. Watch for sweating, drooling, flushing, cramps, slow pulse, low BP. Avoid in asthma.
Antibiotics
Treat infection
Take the full course, even when symptoms improve.
Urinary analgesic
Treat pain and burning
Pyridium (phenazopyridine): turns urine orange-red and can stain clothes and contacts. Slightly sedating. Treats pain, not infection; usually about 2 days.
Urinary antispasmodic
Treat bladder spasms
Myrbetriq (mirabegron), which relaxes the bladder: significant side effects. It can raise BP, so monitor it.

sections.example: At the bedside: Four days after starting Ditropan for urgency, an 81-year-old is newly confused. She has not had a bowel movement in 4 days. You feel a firm bladder above the pubic bone. These are anticholinergic effects. You hold the next dose, do a bladder scan, and notify the provider.

sections.heading: How do you give diuretics safely?
sections.keyIdea: Check BUN, creatinine, potassium, sodium, and BP before every diuretic dose, and give it in the morning.
sections.body:
Diuretics make the kidneys remove more water and sodium, so urine output rises. They treat high BP, heart failure, and fluid overload.

Loop and thiazide diuretics make the body lose potassium. A potassium-sparing diuretic keeps it. Most salt substitutes are potassium chloride, so a client on Aldactone should not use them.

rows: Loop
Lasix (furosemide)
BUN, Cr, K⁺, Na⁺. Strong; causes potassium loss.
Thiazide
HCTZ (hydrochlorothiazide)
BUN, Cr, K⁺, Na⁺. Also causes potassium loss.
Potassium-sparing
Aldactone (spironolactone)
Same labs. Keeps potassium. No salt substitutes.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor; osmotic
Acetazolamide; mannitol
Used in special cases, such as glaucoma or brain swelling. Watch I&O and electrolytes.

steps: Check BUN, creatinine, K⁺, and Na⁺ first. Report low K⁺ with Lasix or HCTZ, or high K⁺ with Aldactone, before the dose.
Check BP. Diuretics can lower it and cause dizziness on standing.
Monitor I&O and daily weight: same time, same scale, same clothing.
Give it in the morning when possible, so the client is not up all night.
Keep a urinal or commode and the call light in reach to prevent falls.
sections.example: At the bedside: A client due for Lasix 40 mg has a potassium of 3.1 mEq/L and a BP of 98/58. You hold the dose and notify the provider. More Lasix would lower both further. For another client on Aldactone with a potassium of 5.8 mEq/L, you also hold and notify.

check.q: A client on Aldactone switched to a salt substitute to cut sodium. What do you say?
check.a: Stop the substitute. It is made of potassium, and Aldactone already holds potassium in, so the level could rise too high.

sections.heading: How do the two types of dialysis differ?
sections.keyIdea: Dialysis removes wastes and fluid when the kidneys cannot, and it must be repeated often.
sections.body:
Your slides describe dialysis as therapy for severely reduced or absent kidney function. It removes wastes and extra fluid the kidneys can no longer clear. It must be done at frequent intervals, because wastes and fluid build up again.

For a fistula, a missing thrill or bruit means it may be clotted. That needs immediate follow-up.

rows: How it works
Blood flows through an outside machine that filters it, then returns to the body.
Solution goes into the abdomen. The belly lining acts as the filter, and then the fluid is drained.
Access
A fistula or graft in the arm, or a special catheter
A catheter into the abdomen
Where and how often
Usually at a center, about three times a week
Usually at home, every day
Key nursing points
No BP, blood draws, or IVs in the fistula arm. Check for a thrill and bruit.
Strict aseptic technique. Cloudy drained fluid, fever, or belly pain suggests infection; report it.

sections.analogy: Hemodialysis is like taking a car's oil out, running it through an outside filter, and pouring it back. Peritoneal dialysis is like pouring cleaning solution into the engine, letting it soak up grime, and draining it out.

sections.heading: What habits prevent urinary problems?
sections.keyIdea: Healthy weight, enough fluid, fiber, no straining, no delay, fewer irritants, and no smoking protect the bladder.
sections.body: Your slides list healthy habits that prevent urinary and bowel problems. These are the core of client teaching. Teach them in plain words and check understanding.
bullets: Keep a healthy weight and exercise. Extra weight presses on the bladder and weakens the pelvic floor.
Do not delay voiding. Go when the urge comes.
Do not use the pelvic floor muscles to force urine out (straining).
Drink enough fluid and eat a high-fiber diet. Treat constipation or diarrhea as it occurs; a full rectum presses on the bladder.
Avoid bladder irritants, such as caffeine, alcohol, and artificial sweeteners.
Do not smoke. Smoking irritates the bladder, and chronic cough strains the pelvic floor.

check.q: A client drinks very little at work so she will not have to void. Why is this a problem?
check.a: Low intake makes urine concentrated. That irritates the bladder and raises infection risk. Teach her to spread fluids through the day.

sections.heading: Common traps: look-alikes to tell apart
sections.keyIdea: Most errors come from mixing up opposite drug actions or treating a symptom drug as a cure.

rows: Anticholinergic vs cholinergic
Anti (Ditropan) calms the bladder and can cause retention. Cholinergic (Urecholine) makes it empty.
Pyridium vs antibiotic
Pyridium only numbs the pain. The antibiotic cures the infection and must be finished.
Potassium-losing vs potassium-sparing
Lasix and HCTZ lose K⁺; hold for low K⁺. Aldactone keeps K⁺; hold for high K⁺.
Hemodialysis vs peritoneal
Hemo: blood to a machine, at a center. Peritoneal: solution in the belly, daily at home.
Routine catheter fix vs infection
A kinked tube is a quick fix. Fever and flank pain need assessment and a prompt report.
Orange urine: danger vs expected
On Pyridium, orange-red urine is expected. Reassure the client.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Expect "hold or give" drug items, safety-cue spotting with aides, and teaching checks on new drugs.
sections.body:
Sample: A 73-year-old with heart failure is due for furosemide (Lasix) 40 mg IV at 0900. Today's potassium is 3.1 mEq/L, and BP is 98/58. What should the nurse do?

A. Give the dose and recheck BP in 30 minutes
B. Hold the dose and notify the provider
C. Give half the dose
D. Give the dose with a glass of orange juice
bullets: Hold or give: compare labs and BP with the drug's main risk.
Clarify an order: Ditropan for a client with glaucoma.
Aide actions: a bag above the bladder needs you to step in.
Teaching: Pyridium color, finishing antibiotics, no salt substitutes.
Dialysis: an absent thrill, cloudy drainage, a protected arm.
steps: Read the stem: a loop diuretic is due, with a low potassium and a low BP.
What is it really asking? Is it safe to give this drug now?
Key cues: Lasix lowers potassium and BP. Both are already low.
Why the others are wrong: A and D still give a drug that makes both worse. C changes the dose without an order.
The answer is B. Hold and notify the provider.
Strategy: before any diuretic, ask, "Would this dose push a low number lower?" If yes, hold and report.

sections.heading: Worked case: new confusion after a bladder drug
sections.keyIdea: In an older adult, new confusion, constipation, or retention after an anticholinergic means hold, assess, and report.
sections.body: An 81-year-old started Ditropan 4 days ago for urgency. Today she is confused and restless. She has had no bowel movement in 4 days. Her mouth is dry, and she has a firm, rounded swelling above the pubic bone.
steps: Recognize cues: new confusion, constipation, dry mouth, and a full bladder.
Analyze: all are anticholinergic effects. Older adults are at higher risk.
Prioritize: retention can harm the bladder and add to her confusion.
Act: hold the next dose. Do a bladder scan.
Report the findings and the scan result to the provider.
Evaluate: watch output, bowel function, and mental status after changes.

check.q: Which other client should not get Ditropan without clarifying the order?
check.a: A client with glaucoma. Anticholinergics can raise eye pressure.

pearls: Bag below the bladder, system closed, catheter out as soon as it is not needed.
Unless fluids are restricted, encourage about 2 L or more a day, spread out.
Ditropan: avoid in glaucoma; watch older adults for retention, constipation, and confusion.
Pyridium turns urine orange-red and stains contacts. It does not cure infection.
Diuretics: check labs first, weigh daily, give in the morning, prevent falls.
Myrbetriq can raise BP. Monitor it.
redFlags: Potassium out of range before a diuretic dose → hold and notify the provider.
Confusion, constipation, or a full bladder after starting an anticholinergic → hold the dose, assess for retention, and report.
Absent thrill or bruit over a fistula → immediate follow-up.
Cloudy peritoneal drainage, fever, or belly pain → suspect infection and notify the provider.
Fever, flank pain, or cloudy, foul urine with a catheter → report; possible catheter infection.

checks.q: A client is alarmed that his urine is bright orange after starting a drug for burning. Which drug is likely?
checks.a: Pyridium (phenazopyridine). Reassure him it is expected, and warn that it can stain clothes and contact lenses.

checks.q: Which two diuretics cause potassium loss, and which one spares it?
checks.a: Lasix and HCTZ cause potassium loss. Aldactone is potassium-sparing.

checks.q: On day 2, a client stops the antibiotic because "the burning is gone" with Pyridium. What do you teach?
checks.a: Pyridium only masks pain. The infection is still there, so finish the full antibiotic course.

checks.q: A client on bethanechol voids well and has a low residual on scan. What does this show?
checks.a: The drug is working. It is meant to help the bladder empty.

checks.q: Which actions protect a new AV fistula in the right arm?
checks.a: No BP, blood draws, or IVs in that arm. Check daily for a thrill and bruit.

checks.q: Which items count as intake for a client on strict I&O?
checks.a: Oral fluids, foods liquid at room temperature such as gelatin or ice chips, IV fluids, and tube feedings.

topics.title: Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
topics.summary: Kidneys and bladders change from birth to old age. Knowing what is normal at each stage helps you spot what is not.
objectives: You can describe normal newborn kidney function and when a newborn should first void.
You can state when children gain bladder control and when bedwetting becomes a concern.
You can explain urinary changes in pregnancy and after birth, including glycosuria and UTI risk.
You can explain why older adults face more dehydration, drug toxicity, nocturia, and low sodium.
You can plan age-appropriate assessment and teaching for each stage.
topics.bigPicture:
The kidneys do the same job at every age, but how well they do it changes. At birth they are immature. In pregnancy they are pushed hard. In later life they slowly lose function. The bladder changes too. It goes from small and frequent in infancy, to learned control in childhood, to holding less in old age.

For the nurse, the key question is always: is this normal for this age, or a problem? Bedwetting at 5 is normal. At 10 it needs a closer look. Waking once at night to void is common at 80. Leaking urine is not.
recap: Newborns have a lower GFR and cannot concentrate or dilute urine well. Watch for dehydration and overhydration.
Newborns void within 24 hours and must void by 48 hours. No void by 48 hours is reported.
Most children gain control between 2 and 5 years. Daytime control comes before nighttime control.
Bedwetting is not a problem until after age 7. Daytime wetting may be pathologic.
Pregnancy: frequency early, eases in the 2nd trimester, returns in the 3rd. GFR rises up to 50%.
Glycosuria in pregnancy may be normal or may signal gestational diabetes. Report and follow up.
Postpartum: overdistention, incomplete emptying, residual urine, and UTI risk. A full bladder can increase bleeding.
Older adults: dilute urine, nocturia, slower drug clearance, dehydration and low sodium risk. Incontinence is never normal.

keyTerms.def: How much blood the kidneys filter per minute. Lower in newborns, higher in pregnancy, lower with aging.
To save water by making a small amount of strong, dark urine.
Involuntary passing of urine, especially by a child old enough to have bladder control.
Bedwetting during sleep.
Daytime wetting. It may be pathologic, a sign of an underlying problem.
Caused by disease or a body problem, not part of normal growth.
Glucose in the urine.
High blood glucose that first appears during pregnancy.
The top of the uterus. After birth, it should be firm and midline.
Urine that stays in the bladder after voiding.
Stretching of the bladder beyond its normal size because it is not emptied.
Making large amounts of urine, as in the first days after birth.
Stiff from extra tough tissue. An older bladder becomes more fibrous and holds less.
A low sodium level in the blood.

sections.heading: Why are newborn kidneys different?
sections.keyIdea: Newborn kidneys cannot adjust quickly, so small changes in fluid can cause dehydration or overload.
sections.body:
A newborn's kidneys work, but not at full strength. Your slides note the GFR is lower than an adult's. Newborns also have limits in concentrating and diluting urine.

In plain words, they cannot hold on to water well when short of it. They also cannot get rid of extra water quickly. That is why watching for dehydration and overhydration matters so much. A small error in IV fluids has a big effect.
sections.analogy: An adult's kidneys are like a skilled cook who can make a soup stronger or weaker on demand. A newborn's kidneys are a trainee who makes it one way. That is fine on a normal day, but slow to adjust when something changes.
sections.example: At the bedside: A 2-day-old on IV fluids for poor feeding has the pump running at twice the prescribed rate. The baby's kidneys cannot quickly get rid of the extra fluid. First, stop or correct the infusion. Then assess the baby and report the error.

sections.heading: When should a newborn first void?
sections.keyIdea: Healthy newborns void within 24 hours, and they must void by 48 hours after birth.
sections.body: Your slides set clear limits. Most newborns void in the first day. A baby who has not voided by 48 hours may have a kidney or urinary tract problem. The provider needs to know.
bullets: Healthy newborns void within the first 24 hours.
Make sure the newborn voids within 48 hours after delivery. If not, report it.
If a newborn has not voided, assess fluid intake, bladder distention, restlessness, and pain.
Voiding is more frequent than in older children, since the bladder is small and urine is not concentrated.
Urine may be cloudy in the newborn. It becomes straw-colored in early infancy.
sections.example: At the bedside: A breastfed newborn is 30 hours old with no wet diapers. You review how often and how well the baby feeds. You gently feel for a full bladder above the pubic bone. You watch for restlessness or pain. You document carefully and report, knowing 48 hours is the key limit.

check.q: A parent worries that a 1-day-old's urine looks cloudy. The baby feeds well and has voided twice. What do you say?
check.a: Cloudy urine can be normal in a newborn. It becomes straw-colored in early infancy.

sections.heading: When do children gain bladder control?
sections.keyIdea: Most children gain control between ages 2 and 5, daytime first; bedwetting is not a concern until after 7.
sections.body:
Your slides say most children gain urinary control between 2 and 5 years. Daytime control comes before nighttime control. A child who is dry all day but wets at night is following the normal order.

Toilet learning is more than control. Young children need reminders about flushing and handwashing. They also need help learning to wipe. Teaching girls to wipe front to back keeps germs from the anus away from the urethra.

From 5 to 10, the kidneys double in size. A school-age child voids 6 to 8 times a day. Wetting, called enuresis, is common at this age.

rows: Nocturnal enuresis (bedwetting)
Wetting during sleep. Common in deep sleepers, who do not wake to a full bladder.
Not a problem until after age 7. Formal definitions use the word from age 5, but most children outgrow it, so treatment usually does not start before about age 6 or 7.
Diurnal enuresis (daytime wetting)
Wetting while awake
May be pathologic. It can point to infection, constipation, a structural problem, or stress, so it needs evaluation.

sections.example: At the bedside: A parent says her 6-year-old wets the bed a few nights a week and is "impossible to wake up." He is dry all day. You reassure her this is common and not a problem until after age 7. You suggest fewer drinks in the evening and voiding before bed.

check.q: A 9-year-old who has been dry for years starts wetting his pants at school. Is this expected?
check.a: No. Daytime wetting may be pathologic. He needs evaluation for causes such as infection, constipation, or stress.

sections.heading: How does pregnancy change urination?
sections.keyIdea: Frequency comes and goes with the position of the uterus, and higher GFR can spill glucose into the urine.
sections.body:
Pregnancy changes urination in two ways: pressure and kidney workload. The growing uterus presses on the bladder, so the client voids more often. The steps show the pattern on your slides.

GFR rises early in pregnancy. It reaches as much as 50% above normal by the second trimester and stays high until birth. To keep up, the tubules take back more. But when too much glucose is filtered, some spills into the urine. That is glycosuria. It may be normal, or it may signal gestational diabetes. Report it so blood glucose can be checked.

Teach the warning signs of a UTI, such as burning, urgency, fever, or flank pain.
steps: First trimester: the uterus is still in the pelvis, against the bladder, so frequency rises.
Second trimester: the uterus rises into the abdomen, so frequency eases.
Third trimester: the baby drops lower into the pelvis, so frequency returns.
sections.analogy: Picture workers taking boxes (glucose) off a conveyor belt and putting them back on the shelf. In pregnancy, the belt speeds up by half. The workers move faster, but some boxes still fall off the end, into the urine.

check.q: At 34 weeks, a client says, "I'm voiding all the time again. It got better for a few months." Is something wrong?
check.a: This is expected. Frequency eases in the second trimester and returns in the third. Teach her the signs of a UTI.

sections.heading: What happens to the bladder after birth?
sections.keyIdea: After birth, the bladder may fill fast and empty poorly, and a full bladder can push the uterus aside and increase bleeding.
sections.body:
After birth, the bladder and urethra are stretched and bruised. An epidural may still dull the urge. Meanwhile, the body sheds the extra fluid of pregnancy, so the bladder fills fast.

Large voids on the first day are expected diuresis when the fundus is firm and midline. Small, frequent voids with a feeling of fullness are not. They suggest the bladder is not emptying.
bullets: Overdistention of the bladder.
Incomplete emptying and residual urine.
UTI: urine that sits is a good place for germs, and catheters during labor add risk.
Urine output rises in the early postpartum period.
Signs of a full bladder: fundus pushed up and to one side, a bulge above the pubic bone, small frequent voids, and heavier bleeding.
sections.example: At the bedside: Four hours after a vaginal birth with an epidural, a client has not voided. Her fundus is above the navel and pushed to the right, with a soft bulge above the pubic bone. A full bladder keeps the uterus from contracting well. You help her to the bathroom first. If she cannot void, follow protocol for a bladder scan or catheter.

sections.heading: How do kidneys change with age?
sections.keyIdea: Aging kidneys get less blood, clear drugs slowly, and lose water easily, so dehydration and toxicity come faster.
sections.body:
Your slides describe several changes in the aging kidney. Each change explains a risk you will see on the floor. Read the table as cause on the left and result on the right.

Because drugs clear slowly, question a standard adult dose of a kidney-cleared drug when kidney function is low.

rows: Less blood flow to the kidneys, because the vessels that supply them shrink
Lower GFR. The kidneys clear wastes and drugs more slowly.
Less ability to concentrate urine; urine is more dilute
Higher risk of dehydration. The kidneys keep losing water even when the body is short.
More fluid and electrolytes excreted at night
More urine at night can interrupt sleep (nocturia) and lead to falls.
Impaired drug excretion
Higher risk of overdose and side effects. Doses often need to be lower.
Trouble regulating sodium and water
Higher risk of hyponatremia (low blood sodium)

check.q: An 88-year-old with a creatinine clearance of 38 mL/min is prescribed the standard adult dose of a kidney-cleared antibiotic. What do you do?
check.a: Question the dose with the provider or pharmacist. Low kidney function slows drug removal, so toxicity is more likely.

sections.heading: How does the aging bladder change?
sections.keyIdea: An older bladder holds less, empties less fully, and warns later, and diuretics make these changes worse.
sections.body: The bladder and its controls change too. These changes make urgency, nocturia, and leftover urine more common. Even so, remember: incontinence and acute retention are never a normal part of aging.
bullets: The bladder becomes more fibrous (stiffer). It holds less and leaves more residual urine, which raises UTI risk.
Less autonomic control of the bladder. The urge may come later and more suddenly.
Weaker pelvic floor muscles, so it is harder to hold urine.
Diuretics for high BP or heart disease make these problems worse. They add to trouble concentrating urine and balancing electrolytes.
sections.example: At the bedside: An 86-year-old on HCTZ gets up three times a night to void. She has had two near-falls, and her sodium is low. Aging kidneys plus a diuretic explain both. You place a night-light and a bedside commode, encourage fluids earlier in the day, and report the sodium.

sections.heading: How can you protect older adults' urinary health?
sections.keyIdea: Focus on daytime fluids, medication review, scheduled toileting, fall prevention, and close monitoring.
sections.body:
Older adults lose water easily, clear drugs slowly, and void more at night. So the nurse focuses on hydration, medication safety, sleep, and fall prevention.

Signs of trouble may be subtle. With dehydration or a UTI, an older adult may show new confusion, weakness, or a fall instead of thirst or burning.
steps: Encourage fluids during the day, unless restricted. Taper them in the evening to reduce nocturia without causing dehydration.
Review medicines with the provider and pharmacist. Kidney-cleared drugs may need lower doses. Diuretics are best taken in the morning.
Offer the toilet on a schedule, such as every 2 to 3 hours while awake.
Prevent falls at night: a night-light, a clear path, a bedside commode or urinal, and the call light in reach.
Monitor I&O, daily weight, and labs such as sodium, BUN, and creatinine. Report changes.
sections.example: At the bedside: A 90-year-old who usually chats at breakfast is drowsy and confused. Her water pitcher is still full from yesterday. Her urine is dark amber, and the specific gravity is 1.032. You suspect dehydration. You offer fluids and report the change in mental status. The plan adds her favorite drinks every hour while awake.

sections.heading: Common traps: look-alikes to tell apart
sections.keyIdea: The same finding can be normal at one age and a red flag at another, so always check the age first.

rows: First void at 24 hours vs 48 hours
Expect it by 24 hours. No void by 48 hours is reported.
Bedwetting vs daytime wetting
Bedwetting is fine until after age 7. Daytime wetting may be pathologic.
Normal glycosuria vs gestational diabetes
You cannot tell from the urine. Report it so blood glucose is checked.
Postpartum diuresis vs retention
Large voids with a firm, midline fundus are normal. Small voids, fullness, and a displaced fundus suggest retention.
Normal aging vs not normal
Nocturia, dilute urine, and smaller capacity are normal. Incontinence and acute retention never are.
Confusion from dementia vs new confusion
A sudden change may be dehydration or a UTI. Report it.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Expect "is this normal for this age?" items, priority picks among four clients, and postpartum bladder checks.
sections.body:
Sample: The school nurse reviews four children whose parents are worried about wetting. Which child most needs a referral?

A. A 4-year-old dry by day who wets at night
B. A 6-year-old deep sleeper who wets the bed twice a week
C. An 8-year-old, dry for years, now wetting during the school day
D. A 3-year-old who still needs reminders to flush and wash
bullets: Normal or not: match the finding to the age.
Priority: the newborn with no void at 48 hours, or the older adult with new confusion.
Postpartum: a displaced fundus and a bulge mean help her void first.
Older adults: question standard doses of kidney-cleared drugs.
steps: Read the stem: four children, four ages, four wetting patterns.
What is it really asking? Which pattern is not normal for the age.
Key cues: day vs night, and the child's age compared with 2 to 5 years and 7 years.
Why the others are wrong: A and D are normal toddler learning. B is bedwetting under age 7 in a deep sleeper.
The answer is C. New daytime wetting in a school-age child may be pathologic.
Strategy: first ask, "Day or night?" Then ask, "What age is normal for this?"

sections.heading: Worked case: the older adult on a diuretic
sections.keyIdea: An older adult plus a diuretic plus low fluids leads to dehydration and low sodium; new confusion may be the first sign.
sections.body: An 84-year-old takes HCTZ for high BP. Today she is newly confused. Her mouth is dry. She has been voiding large amounts of pale urine at night. She says she drinks little so she will not have to get up. Her sodium is 128 mEq/L.
steps: Recognize cues: new confusion, dry mouth, night voiding, low intake, and a low sodium.
Analyze: aging kidneys lose water and sodium easily. The thiazide adds to both.
Prioritize: dehydration and hyponatremia are causing the confusion until proven otherwise.
Act: report the confusion and sodium to the provider. Ask about morning dosing.
Plan: daytime fluids she likes, a night-light, a bedside commode, and the call light in reach.
Evaluate: watch mental status, I&O, weight, and sodium.

check.q: Why is "limit her fluids so she sleeps through the night" the wrong plan?
check.a: It worsens dehydration. Give fluids in the daytime and taper them in the evening instead.

pearls: Newborns: no void by 48 hours is reported. Assess intake, distention, restlessness, and pain.
Day control comes before night control. Bedwetting is fine until after age 7.
Pregnancy glycosuria may be normal or gestational diabetes. Always follow up.
Postpartum: a displaced fundus and suprapubic bulge mean a full bladder. Help her void first.
Older adults clear kidney-excreted drugs slowly. Question standard adult doses when kidney function is low.
In older adults, new confusion may be the first sign of dehydration or a UTI.
redFlags: Newborn with no void by 48 hours, a distended bladder, restlessness, or pain → report to the provider.
Newborn IV running faster than ordered → stop or correct the infusion first, then assess and report.
Postpartum client who has not voided, with a full bladder or a displaced, boggy uterus → help her void or follow protocol; bleeding may increase.
Older adult with new confusion, dizziness, or falls on a diuretic → check sodium, potassium, and hydration, and notify the provider.

checks.q: A term newborn is 40 hours old and has not voided. What do you do first?
checks.a: Assess intake, bladder distention, restlessness, and pain. The baby must void by 48 hours, so report findings to the provider.

checks.q: A parent of a 3-year-old worries he is dry all day but wets every night. What do you say?
checks.a: That is expected. Most children gain control between 2 and 5, and daytime control comes first.

checks.q: A pregnant client's dipstick shows glucose. What does this mean?
checks.a: It may be normal, because higher GFR filters more glucose than the tubules take back. It may also be gestational diabetes, so report and follow up.

checks.q: On postpartum day 1, a client voids 500 to 700 mL each time. Her fundus is firm and midline. Is this normal?
checks.a: Yes. Large voids in the early postpartum period are expected diuresis.

checks.q: Name two reasons an older adult has more residual urine.
checks.a: The bladder becomes more fibrous with less capacity. Autonomic control declines, and the pelvic floor weakens.

checks.q: An 80-year-old asks why she now gets up at night to void. She has no burning or leaking. What do you explain?
checks.a: Aging kidneys excrete more fluid at night, so nocturia is common.
